fieldsRead.text: Radboud Biology combines organismal, ecological, molecular and medical biology. Students build a broad foundation, develop research skills and choose a domain before completing a research internship.

The UCR options emphasise broad biological science, environmental biology, or human biology and neuroscience with health psychology. They differ from Radboud’s plant physiology and development, microbial metabolism, extensive domain study and compulsory research internship. UCR optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC and does not guarantee a Biology placement.

The adopted curriculum contains 36 EC of restricted choices and 30 EC of free electives. Choices and the final project require the applicable approval and prior preparation; prospective 2027–2028 overviews may change.

The individual final project is a 12-EC research internship. Entry requires at least 120 EC including the complete first year, and prior project approval. An extension of up to 3 EC uses elective space and must be agreed in the internship plan.
36 EC of restricted choices includes a 30-EC personalised domain from approved BB1/BB2 lists and further restricted electives.
30 EC of assessable academic bachelor electives. BB1/BB2 courses and a coherent minor of 15–30 EC are recommended.

Personal and Professional Development starts in year 1 and is signed off later. Introductory and research skills are embedded in first-year courses; compulsory RADAr adds no credits. The normal first-year study-advice threshold is 39 of 60 EC, subject to personal circumstances.

The broad UCR option combines ecological and human/molecular biology. The environmental option devotes more study to climate, Earth systems, resources and governance; the human option includes substantial health psychology. None reproduces Radboud’s dedicated plant physiology and development, broad microbiology and microbial metabolism, histology, extensive domain specialisation or required research-department internship. Optional UCR independent research is additional to the scheduled 180 EC and is not a guaranteed Biology placement.

Study living systems from biodiversity, evolution and ecosystems to cells, biochemistry, human physiology, genetics and disease. Laboratory work, statistics and data analysis support these biological questions; environmental science, sustainability governance and ethics add complementary perspectives.

Study biodiversity, evolution, ecosystems and conservation alongside climate change and environmental systems. Spatial analysis, soils, biogeochemistry and sustainability research connect ecological questions with environmental assessment; governance, justice and resource geoscience provide complementary approaches.

Study molecular and cellular biology, human physiology, infection, genetics and disease together with neurobiology and cognition. A substantial psychology strand examines behaviour, mental health, development and assessment. Laboratory work, epidemiology, statistics and research synthesis support this combination; it is not a specialist medical or clinical qualification. Normative ethical reasoning complements the biological and psychological inquiry; this is not professional clinical-psychology training.

selectedDescriptions.name: Personal & Professional Development

content.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
content.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
content.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
content.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

selectedDescriptions.name: Introduction to Data Science

content.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
content.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
content.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
content.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

selectedDescriptions.contribution: develops data cleaning, visualisation and computational analysis applicable to biological datasets
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

selectedDescriptions.name: Machine Learning

content.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
content.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
content.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
content.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

selectedDescriptions.contribution: provides regression, classification, clustering and model-validation methods complementary to the environmental route’s analysis of complex measured data; no biological application is guaranteed
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.

selectedDescriptions.name: Building with Nature

content.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
content.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
content.topics: Nature-based infrastructure; Coastal and water management; Walcheren's water-management history; Sandy and muddy coasts; Lowland lakes; Rivers and estuaries; Urban nature-based solutions; Harbour habitats; Habitat connectivity; Ecoducts and fish ladders
content.methods: Building with Nature case analysis; Ecological-corridor project analysis; Nature-based intervention design; Construction and testing of model walls

selectedDescriptions.contribution: examines nature-based systems and ecological responses to environmental risk
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.

selectedDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability

content.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
content.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
content.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
content.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

selectedDescriptions.contribution: examines institutions and collective decisions that shape ecological sustainability
